title: GCD & LCM
description: The greatest common divisor and least common multiple, and the fast Euclidean algorithm

blocks.text: The greatest common divisor (GCD) and least common multiple (LCM) are two of the most useful tools in number theory. They appear in problems about fractions, cycles, tiling, and scheduling.
The best part is that both can be computed in just a few lines using the elegant Euclidean algorithm.
The GCD of two numbers is the largest number that divides both of them exactly. For 12 and 18, the common divisors are 1, 2, 3, and 6, so the GCD is 6.
Intuitively, it is the biggest tile that can perfectly cover both a 12 unit and an 18 unit length. If the GCD is 1, the two numbers share no factors and are called coprime.

items: The largest number dividing both inputs
A GCD of 1 means the numbers are coprime
Also called the greatest common factor

blocks.text: The LCM of two numbers is the smallest positive number that both divide into. For 4 and 6, the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12 and of 6 are 6, 12, so the LCM is 12.
This is the tool for problems where two cycles must line up again, like two blinking lights or two gears returning to the same position.

items: The smallest number that is a multiple of both inputs
Perfect for when two repeating cycles realign
Always at least as large as either input

blocks.text: The clever way to find the GCD is the Euclidean algorithm. It rests on one fact: the GCD of a and b is the same as the GCD of b and the remainder of a divided by b.

blocks.caption: Repeatedly replace the pair with (b, a mod b) until the second number becomes zero

blocks.text: So we repeatedly replace the pair (a, b) with (b, a mod b). The numbers shrink fast, and when the second one hits zero, the first is the answer. It finishes in about log steps, which is extremely fast.

Why it works:

Any number dividing both a and b also divides a mod b, so the set of common divisors never changes as we reduce. The last nonzero value is the greatest of them.
The algorithm translates into a tiny loop or a one line recursion.
Most languages also have this built in, such as std gcd in C++ and math.gcd in Python, but knowing the four line version is essential.

content.title: 5. Getting the LCM from the GCD

blocks.text: You do not compute the LCM directly. Instead you use a beautiful relationship: the product of the GCD and the LCM of two numbers equals the product of the numbers themselves.

blocks.caption: gcd(a, b) times lcm(a, b) equals a times b
blocks.alt: Getting the LCM from the GCD

blocks.text: Rearranging gives the LCM as a times b, divided by the GCD. Divide first to avoid overflow on large inputs.

codes.python:
def lcm(a, b):
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b               # divide first to avoid overflow

blocks.text: GCD and LCM turn up in many disguises.

items: Reducing a fraction to lowest terms by dividing by the GCD
Finding when two repeating events happen together using the LCM
Checking whether numbers are coprime, meaning GCD is 1
Tiling and grid problems that depend on common factors

blocks.text: Whenever a problem talks about sharing factors or cycles lining up, reach for GCD or LCM first.
